The Continental Army. This was the military force raised by the thirteen colonies and maintained by the Continental Congress during the American Revolution from seventeen seventy-five to seventeen eighty-three. Initially a ragtag militia of volunteers and irregulars, it evolved through warfare and discipline into a professional standing army capable of defeating the British Empire and establishing the independence of the United States.

Established formally by the Continental Congress in June seventeen seventy-five and commanded throughout the war by George Washington, the Continental Army began with fewer than fifteen thousand men and never exceeded thirty thousand at full strength, dwarfed by British and Hessian forces. Recruitment relied on patriotic volunteers, state militia rotations, and later impressment. Soldiers were poorly equipped, paid irregularly, and faced constant supply shortages, yet maintained cohesion through seven years of war.

The army's victories at Trenton in December seventeen seventy-six, Saratoga from September to October seventeen seventy-seven, and Yorktown from September to October seventeen eighty-one were achieved through tactical skill, strategic positioning, and sheer endurance rather than numerical superiority. After the winter ordeal at Valley Forge from seventeen seventy-seven to seventeen seventy-eight and training reforms by Baron von Steuben, the Continental Army emerged as a disciplined force capable of conventional warfare against European regulars.

The army's survival depended on French military aid after seventeen seventy-eight, foreign volunteers, state militias, and supply networks. Internal conflicts between the Congress and Washington over resources and strategy persisted throughout the war. At war's end, many Continental soldiers were unpaid, mutinied for back wages especially in Pennsylvania and New Jersey, and pressured Congress to honor promised pensions, establishing a pattern of veteran discontent after American wars.
